newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish left support PM, despite Rushdie affair.
newsitem.headline: Danish left support PM, despite Rushdie affair.

text.p: Danish left-wing parties with the balance of power in parliament united on Thursday in support of the minority government, threatened with a no-confidence vote over its handling of a planned visit by author Salman Rushdie.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa or death sentence against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.

Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen's political opponents initially suspected that the government's claim, that it could not guarantee Rushdie's security if he went ahead with plans to collect a European Union literary prize, could have been an effort to appease important trade partner, Iran.

"I now see the case as solely one in which Nyrup and his people have bungled and a blunder is not something on which we would topple the government," Socialist People's Party leader Holger Nielsen said. Nielsen told the daily Det Fri Aktuelt he was now satisfied the centre-left coalition had acted out of incompetence and not because it had a secret agenda to keep the author out.
The leftist Unity List has been reluctant to help oust the prime minister throughout the affair.

Its chairman Soeren Soendergaard, agreeing with Nielsen, said: "There have been a sufficient number of mistakes to create a very poor impression but there is nothing on which one can bring down a government."

Iran is traditionally a major buyer of Danish feta-type cheese, importing 1.2 billion crowns worth in 1991-92, although sales have fallen back recently because of importers' bad debts which Danish producers are trying to recover.
But after attending a session of the secret parliamentary intelligence supervisory committee on Wednesday Nielsen said he had received assurances there had been a real security threat to Rushdie.

Denied a majority without the left, the rightist camp will now drop its plan to oust Nyrup but is likely to win cross-party support for harsh criticism of the government at a debate next week, political sources from both sides said.
Nielsen has described the government's handling of the affair as "incompetent to the most unbelievable degree".
Author Rushdie was confusingly informed of the entry ban in a press statement, while his associates were still in talks with Danish authorities on a trip they thought had been approved.
Rasmussen said prior public knowledge of Rushdie's plans to attend the award ceremony on November 14 put his safety in Copenhagen, the 1996 European Cultural Capital, in jeopardy.

Following an outcry at home and abroad the prime minister apologised and said the intention had been to offer the author an alternative date to receive his prize. This detail had been omitted however from the message to Rushdie.
